turns.prompt_text: I made this corner joint by cutting after measuring them perfectly I do not want to use that again I would prefer to make a template so that I can set a circular saw and just push eye this to the circular saw or the plank into the Attached 1 file. - cc59e88b-f42d-4f91-a206-1aab7ff6169a
turns.response_html:
That looks like a solid, clean box joint (also called a finger joint). Measuring and marking every single one of those fingers by hand is an absolute test of patience, so it makes total sense that you want a repeatable way to batch them out.

Using a handheld circular saw for box joints is a bit unconventional compared to using a table saw or a router, but you can absolutely create a repeatable template/jig system to make the cuts fast and accurate without marking every board.

Here are the best ways to set up a template system for this:

Option 1: The "Step-Block" Guide Rail Template

If you are using a handheld circular saw, you cannot easily use a traditional sliding pin jig. Instead, you need a fixed template that guides the baseplate of your saw at perfectly spaced intervals.

  1. Build a Master Template Guide: Take a straight piece of plywood to act as your guide rail. Attach a series of perfectly spaced wooden blocks (teeth) along the top of it.
  2. The Spacing Formula: The gap between each block needs to equal the exact width of your saw's baseplate (from the edge of the baseplate to the blade) plus the width of the finger you want to cut.
  3. How it works: You clamp this master template across your workpiece. You make a pass with the saw running against the first block, move the saw to the next slot, and make the next pass.
  4. Clearing the waste: You will need to make a few closely spaced passes within the pin area to clear out the wood, then clean up the bottom of the joint with a chisel.

Option 2: The Inverted Circular Saw "Table Saw" Jig

If by "pushing the plank into the saw" you mean mounting your circular saw upside down under a workbench to act as a makeshift table saw, you can build the classic Box Joint Jig.

⚠️ Safety Note: Inverting a circular saw requires rock-solid mounting, a reliable power switch override, and extreme caution since there is no splitting wedge/riving knife.

If you go this route, the classic Pin Jig is the golden standard:

  • The Setup: You attach a runner to a small crosscut sled that rides in a slot next to the blade.
  • The Index Pin: You place a small wooden key (the exact width of your blade's kerf or the finger size, depending on your setup) next to the blade. The distance between the blade and the pin must exactly equal the width of the finger.
  • How it works: You make your first cut, then slide that freshly cut notch over the indexing pin. The pin positions the board perfectly for the next cut. Repeat down the line. No measuring required after the initial setup.

Option 3: The Multi-Board Clamping Trick

If you want to stick to a handheld circular saw without building a complex jig:

  1. Clamp all four of your box sides tightly together in a bunch, faces aligned.
  2. Mark the finger locations once across the top edges of the entire bundle.
  3. Set your circular saw depth to the exact thickness of the wood.
  4. Cut across all the boards at the same time using a single straight-edge guide clamped down.

Are you planning to use the circular saw handheld with a guide rail system, or are you looking to build a makeshift table saw setup where the blade is stationary?

turns.prompt_text: I am looking to invest into a Ryobi table Saw that I plug into an outlet So then I would be able to use the template much easier
turns.response_html:
Upgrading to a dedicated, corded table saw will make a night-and-day difference for a project like this. Instead of fighting a handheld tool and worrying about depth control, a table saw gives you a perfectly flat surface, consistent cutting height, and standard miter tracks to build a proper crosscut sled jig.

If you are looking at Ryobi's corded lineup, they offer models like the 10" Compact Table Saw (RTS12) or the 10" Expanded Capacity Table Saw (RTS23). Both feature a standard 15-Amp motor, providing more than enough power to batch out clean joints without bogging down.

Here is how you can set up a flawless, zero-measurement template jig using your new table saw.

The Crosscut Sled Index-Pin Jig

This is the gold standard for box joints. Once it is calibrated, you can cut dozens of fingers without a tape measure, and they will fit together perfectly.

Step 1: Build a Basic Sled

  1. Cut a piece of $\frac{3}{4}\text{-inch}$ plywood to act as the base of a small crosscut sled.
  2. Attach a wooden runner to the bottom of the plywood that fits snugly into one of the table saw’s miter slots, allowing it to slide smoothly forward and backward without side-to-side play.
  3. Screw a sturdy wooden fence across the back edge of the plywood, perpendicular to the blade.
  4. Push the sled through the blade to create a "zero-clearance" slot through the base and fence.

Step 2: Make the Indexing Key

  1. The width of your joint's fingers depends on the thickness of your blade (or dado stack). If you are using a standard single blade, your fingers will match the blade's kerf (usually around $\frac{1}{8}\text{ inch}$). If you want thicker fingers like the ones in your photo, you will want to stack multiple passes or use a dedicated dado blade.
  2. Cut a small, square wooden pin (the indexing key) that matches the exact width of the cut your blade makes.

Step 3: Calibrate the Template

This is the only step that requires precision.

  1. Attach a secondary scrap piece of wood to your sled's fence.
  2. Run the sled through the blade to cut a slot in this scrap piece.
  3. Move the scrap piece over, and glue your indexing key into that slot.
  4. The Magic Distance: Adjust the placement so that the distance between the blade and the indexing key is exactly equal to the width of the key itself. Screw this piece firmly to your main sled fence.

How to Batch Cut the Fingers

Once that key is locked in, the work becomes incredibly fast and mechanical:

  • Board A: Place the edge of your first plank flush against the indexing key. Hold it tight against the fence and slide the sled forward to make your first cut. Take the plank off, place that brand-new notch right over the indexing key, and make your second cut. Repeat down the length of the board.
  • Board B (The Matching Side): To make the matching offset fingers so the corners interlock, you just need to offset the second board by one full finger width before starting. Use a scrap cutoff piece placed against the indexing key to establish that initial gap, clamp your second board down, and repeat the sliding process.

Using a corded table saw means you can keep the blade set at a depth that matches the exact thickness of your timber, giving you perfectly flush corner joints every single time.

Are you planning to stick with a standard $\frac{1}{8}\text{-inch}$ single blade for smaller fingers, or are you looking to use a dado blade configuration to match the larger width of the joint in your photo?

turns.prompt_text: Can I use a dado blade with a Ryobi table saw?
turns.response_html:
Yes, but with strict limitations. Ryobi's corded 10-inch portable table saws (like the RTS12 and RTS23) do officially support stacked dado blades, but because they are lightweight jobsite saws, their arbors (the threaded shaft that holds the blade) are shorter than what you would find on a massive cabinet saw.

Before you buy a dado set for a Ryobi saw, you need to follow these specific rules to keep it safe and functional:

1. You Must Use a 6-Inch Dado Stack

Even though it is a 10-inch table saw, Ryobi explicitly specifies that you must use a 6-inch diameter stacked dado set (with a standard 5/8-inch arbor hole).

  • Do not buy an 8-inch dado stack. A 6-inch stack requires less power from the motor to spin, which keeps the saw from bogging down or overheating. Because box joints are shallow cuts, a 6-inch blade gives you more than enough height.

2. Maximum Width is 1/2 Inch

The arbor shaft on these saws is only long enough to safely support a stack up to 1/2-inch wide.

  • When you stack the blades and chippers on the shaft, the outer nut must be able to thread onto the arbor completely so that the threads fully engage.
  • Tip from the field: Woodworkers using this saw often have to leave off the thick factory outer washer to gain enough exposed thread for the nut to lock down tightly against a full 1/2-inch stack. Never force a stack that leaves the nut only half-threaded.

3. Absolutely No "Wobble" Blades

Ryobi specifies that you must only use a stacked dado set (which consists of two outer blades and flat chipper blades sandwiched in between). Do not use an adjustable single-blade "wobble" dado or molding cutters. The severe vibration of a wobble blade can damage the motor bearings on a portable saw.

4. You Will Need a Dado Throat Plate

The standard red plastic throat plate that comes in the box only has a narrow slot for a single 1/8-inch blade. If you put a wider dado stack on, it will hit the plastic. You will either need to purchase the matching Ryobi Dado Throat Plate accessory or custom-make your own zero-clearance insert plate out of thin plywood or MDF.

What this means for your template jig:

If the box joint fingers you want to cut are 1/2 inch or less, you can build the crosscut pin jig exactly as described, load up your 6-inch dado stack to match that exact width, and blast out the fingers in a single pass per notch. It makes the entire process incredibly fast!

turns.prompt_text: This whole NATO setup sounds like a lot of pieces and set up whilst the total cost on this
turns.response_html:
It definitely sounds like a lot of moving parts when you list it all out, but once the jig is put together, it's just a mechanical "slide and cut" process.

As for the total damage to your wallet, you can actually set this up fairly reasonably. If you buy everything new, here is the breakdown of what the total setup will run you:

1. The Table Saw: $150 – $230

Your upfront cost depends on whether you want a built-in stand or are happy setting the tool directly on a sturdy workbench:

  • Option A (No Stand): The Ryobi 8-1/4" Compact Table Saw (RTS08) sits right on a benchtop and runs about $149. (Note: It is a smaller saw, so check arbor capacity if you plan to upgrade to dado blades down the road).
  • Option B (With Stand): The Ryobi 10" Jobsite Table Saw with a Folding Stand (RTS12) is the sweet spot for general garage use and runs about $229.

2. The Dado Stack & Throat Plate: $65 – $120

If you want to cut those wider fingers in a single pass instead of making multiple cuts with a standard single blade, you will need the matching accessories:

  • 6-Inch Stacked Dado Set: A budget-friendly but solid 6-inch stacked dado blade set (like WEN or Oshlun) runs between $45 and $90.
  • Dado Throat Plate: A factory Ryobi dado insert plate usually runs around $20 to $30. (Budget hack: You can skip buying this entirely and make your own out of a scrap piece of 1/4-inch plywood or MDF for $0).

3. The Template Sled: ~$15 or Free

You don't buy a box joint jig—you build it! All it takes is a small scrap piece of 3/4-inch plywood for the base, a couple of straight hardwood scraps for the fences/runners, and some wood glue/screws. If you don't have scrap wood lying around, a single small "handy panel" of plywood from the hardware store will cost about $15.

Total Estimated Investment:

  • The "Bare Bones" Route: Single standard blade (multiple passes per finger) + Benchtop Saw + Homebuilt Sled = ~$165
  • The "Efficiency" Route: 10" Saw with Stand + 6" Dado Stack + Custom Sled = ~$290 – $340

It's a bit of an investment upfront, but considering it turns a two-hour headache of precision measuring into a 5-minute batch job, it pays for itself fast if you plan on building more boxes, drawers, or furniture.

Do you already have some scrap plywood lying around that you could harvest for the sled, or would you be starting completely from scratch?
